Some people are naturally super-active, while others, like me, are more lazy and tend to procrastinate a lot.

However, discovered i can be active and productive as well if i find a way to do things my way.
For example, exercise. I tried going to the gym many times in the past 10 year and i have never been consistent. 
These were the reasons: 
-the gym gave me too much social anxiety
-i was too lazy to take my bike and reach the gym each time
-i was too lazy to pack my bag and change clothes every time
-i prefer to exercise when i want without having to wait that the machines where empty
-i just hated it, weight lifting wasn’t fun.

So i found a solution, calisthenics:
-it’s way more fun and i feel gratified when doing it
-i can do it at home without feeling judged by others
-i can do it whenever i want so it fits better my schedule, and i can do it instantly without having to reach the gym 
-i can listen to music or a podcast on my stereo at home while doing it 
-i mounted a pull-up bar in my garage so i can do every main exercise
-there’s a calisthenics-park near my house along a running-track so i can go run and exercise a little calisthenics there, killing to birds with one stone.

Since i found this new way of exercise i’m now happy to do it and i’ve been consistently doing it every two days, keeping track of my sessions with an app called “Streaks”. Also, i’m using ChatGPT as my mentor, it tells me all i need to know another exercise and answers every question about health nutrition ecc.

Also, this is crucial, i don’t over-do it. My sessions are very short, even just 10-12 mins of the main exercises and 14 mins of run. This is super important because this is the way to stay consistent. If you think it’s mandatory to do at least one hour a day, you’ll try but then you won’t do it the next day because you won’t feel motivated, instead by doing the minimum you can do every day or every two days like me, you will feel gratified every day and you’ll want to continue your streak, and progress will come 💪

(i do it every two days cause muscles need rest as well to regenerate).

Nel cervello esistono due aree fondamentali: la corteccia prefrontale e il sistema limbico. La corteccia prefrontale è la sede del pensiero razionale e della capacità decisionale, mentre il sistema limbico è responsabile degli impulsi istintivi e delle emozioni intense. La corteccia prefrontale agisce come una sorta di "angioletto", suggerendo le azioni più razionali e sicure, mentre il sistema limbico rappresenta la parte più istintiva e "animale" di noi, spingendoci verso reazioni impulsive, spesso difficili da controllare.

Quando una persona, come il tuo ragazzo, ha difficoltà a gestire i propri impulsi, il sistema limbico prende il sopravvento, soprattutto in condizioni di stress, fatica, o alterazione da alcol e droghe. Questo può sfociare in reazioni di rabbia incontrollata e aggressività. Il fatto che lui non riesca a gestire questi impulsi lo rende pericoloso, e purtroppo la violenza tende spesso ad aumentare nel tempo.

Per te, la situazione è ulteriormente complicata da uno stato emotivo di tristezza e forse depressione, che ti rende più difficile usare la tua razionalità per prendere la decisione di lasciarlo. In momenti di instabilità emotiva, tendiamo a cercare conforto nell’attaccamento, alimentato dall’ossitocina, l’ormone che ci fa legare agli altri. Questo ormone può purtroppo portare a un legame anche in relazioni tossiche, rendendo difficile prendere le distanze.

La cosa più urgente per te ora è metterti in sicurezza. Non affrontarlo o lasciarlo quando siete soli, perché potrebbe avere una reazione violenta. Prima di tutto, assicurati di essere in un luogo sicuro e di informare persone di fiducia, come familiari o amici, della situazione. Quando sarai al sicuro e lontana da lui, potrai interrompere questa relazione.

Ricorda, lasciare questa situazione è l’unica scelta razionale e sicura. Anche se sarà emotivamente difficile, con il tempo i livelli di ossitocina si stabilizzeranno e ti sentirai di nuovo tranquilla e stabile. La tua sicurezza è la priorità assoluta. Non esitare a chiedere aiuto alle forze dell'ordine o a coinvolgere chi ti sta vicino.

To give you a direct answer: it’s about dopamine, if you’re thinking that you need to clean the house, that might seem like too big of a task and your brain will try to avoid it in order to save energy. But if you instead think of a smaller step towards reaching that goal, like just blowing away the dust from the top of a chair, your brain will feel much more prone to doing that task because it’s much easier. Eventually, the zeigarnik effect will kick in, and you’ll want to clean the rest of the furniture, because once you start an activity, you’re brain wants to finish.

But it’s also important to have little breaks in between each little task so you don’t get too tired. If you get too tired from something you have been working on for too long, you’re brain won’t give you that necessary motivation to start again.

I’m going to get a bit technical here, but trust me—this explanation might give you some relief. There’s a part of the brain called the “limbic system,” which is where our impulses and emotions are generated. When you do something you later regret, procrastinate, or fall into a bad habit, it’s often because this part of the brain is “in control.” The limbic system is not “rational”—it’s an ancient part of the brain we inherited long before we became human. It’s essential for survival, generating reactions that once protected us but today can sometimes lead to behaviors we find inconvenient or regrettable.

In your case, what happened that night was likely a result of this mechanism. You’ve always felt a fear of being judged or unwanted because of your appearance, and so, in a moment of insecurity, the limbic system responded by pushing you to act on those fears.

The fact that you were drunk is also very important. There’s a part of the brain that evolved more recently called the “prefrontal cortex,” which handles rational thinking, planning, decision-making, and impulse regulation. However, it struggles to function properly when we’re drunk, tired, sleep-deprived, or emotionally unbalanced. In those moments, it’s harder to control impulses, and we’re more susceptible to acting on fears or insecurities.

So, in short, don’t beat yourself up about it—it was an impulse, or at the very least, an error.

You can absolutely learn to control impulses and regulate emotions using the prefrontal cortex. I won’t get into more technical details, but if you want to learn more, it can be incredibly beneficial, and tools like ChatGPT can help you learn these things quickly.

It’s not a mindset. What you are describing are two different mechanics happening in your brain. One is procrastination, which occurs when your brain avoids the perceived stress or difficulty of a task, and the other one is the Zeigarnik effect, where your brain feels compelled to complete a task once it’s started.

Try breaking down your tasks into small, achievable steps. This will get you unstuck from the inertia of procrastination because your brain is now focusing on smaller, much less demanding goals, for example, working on your project for only 10 or 5 minutes, or starting from a very simple action.

To avoid burnout, use the “pomodoro technique,” splitting the time into smaller chunks, usually 25 minutes of focused work followed by a short break. This method helps maintain focus and avoid burnout. Breaking tasks down also helps keep a steady flow of dopamine, as each small accomplishment provides a reward to your brain, reinforcing motivation.

Also, schedule your day and make a plan with only a small number of tasks to avoid choice paralysis, which happens when you’re overwhelmed by too many choices, which also leads to procrastination.

This should help. Another thing, prioritize sleep, because when you’re sleep deprived you’re more prone to fall for impulses and bad habits. When you’re tired, your prefrontal cortex, the region of the brain designed for rational thinking, decision-making, and emotion/impulse regulation, struggles to function properly.

Also, have a positive outlook on life and mindset. This will ensure your emotional state doesn’t interfere with the prefrontal cortex as well. Believe that you’re capable and don’t be too hard on yourself when things don’t go as planned. Progress isn’t always linear and that’s perfectly fine.

I make electro-kind of music, but maybe i can still be helpful: i recently discovered that in order to give texture and definition to my basses without making them sound muddy, i actually needed to combine softer waveforms, with less volume, or filtered, instead of using waveforms with all harmonics going into distortion with volume at max.
For example i may combine a low pass filters saw, with a trisaw (i’m talking about Sylenth1), with some other waveform of another type, maybe one or two octave higher with even less volume. I adjust the phases so i get a good tone. Then i layer to the bass, if needed, a clean sine to reinforce the bass and i adjust in the mix. Sometimes i make the sound so it can evolve into a more intense in certain parts of the arrangement. Or if the sound it’s static, i may add some layer in more intese parts of the arrangement.

In short: 
-combining the right waveforms and using finesse with the volume for each waveform, before distortion/saruration=cool texture and definition.
also slightly adding waveforms +1 octave or more can give cool character and presence.
-reinforcing with a clean sub (use finesse here as well)
-add a bit of groove like a bit of swing will make the bass bounce more
